title: WebAssembly on the JVM: Feature Evolution, Performance, and the Transition to Endive
gist: Red Hat principal engineer Andrea Peruffo argues WebAssembly has already won the CDN edge (Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai) and is now displacing JNI as the way to embed C/Rust/Python/JavaScript code inside JVM applications, with the Chicory runtime closing the performance gap to native Wasmtime by compiling Wasm to Java bytecode (10x) and then compiling Cranelift itself to Wasm to emit machine assembly (another 10x). He also announces that Chicory is being forked to a new project called Endive under the Bytecode Alliance after talks with Dylibso failed to secure a clean transfer of the name.

themes.theme: Wasm Displacing JNI Inside the JVM

insights.claim: WebAssembly lets a JVM application embed C and Rust libraries while shipping a single fully portable JAR, replacing JNI's requirement to pre-compile a native library for every target OS and CPU architecture.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: The distribution-cost argument, not raw speed, is what moves enterprise Java shops off native bindings; watch for JVM libraries quietly dropping platform-specific artifacts.
insights.quote: When you have JNI, you have to pre-compile your native library for all the target OSs and architectures. But with WebAssembly, you have just one target.
insights.locator: Bringing WebAssembly to the Server Side

insights.claim: Running embedded third-party native libraries inside a WebAssembly sandbox insulates the host program from CVEs in those libraries, because the sandboxed code reaches the system only through a separate API.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Security, not performance, is the wedge that gets Wasm into regulated enterprise stacks; supply-chain risk budgets are the buying trigger.
insights.quote: all your program is protected against the CVEs that the libraries that you are embedding will have
insights.locator: Bringing WebAssembly to the Server Side

insights.claim: Over the past year one engineer shipped databases, CPython, JavaScript engines, protobuf and assorted Rust and C libraries onto the JVM via WebAssembly with only a thin wrapper layer and no rewrites.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: The porting cost of bringing whole foreign ecosystems onto the JVM has collapsed from multi-year rewrites to wrapper work — expect an acceleration in Java-side feature parity.
insights.quote: You can run a ton of really useful things without having to rewrite them.
insights.locator: Last year, I have been able to deliver

insights.claim: The strategic appeal of WebAssembly is that everything built for the browser front end is theoretically reusable server-side unchanged, making it a 'free lunch' reuse platform rather than a new runtime to be bootstrapped.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Server-side Wasm inherits a decade of browser-vendor investment for free; that asymmetry is why it beats greenfield sandbox technologies.
insights.quote: everything that has been developed for WebAssembly in the browser is theoretically reusable over server side
insights.locator: Bringing WebAssembly to the Server Side

themes.theme: The Three-Tier Performance Ladder: Interpreter, Bytecode, Cranelift

insights.claim: A pure WebAssembly interpreter on the JVM is maximally portable — self-contained on the standard library, runnable on Native Image and in the strictest environments — but is inherently slow because instruction-by-instruction dispatch never gives the JVM's C1/C2 JIT anything to optimize.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Portability and speed are separate SKUs in Wasm runtimes; buyers must pick a tier, and vendors that offer only one tier lose deals.
insights.quote: It has to process instructions one by one without a chance of getting JVM C1 or C2, just-in-time compiler, to kick in

insights.claim: Compiling WebAssembly directly to Java bytecode delivered a 10x speedup on the Prism Ruby parser workload, and a newer compiler emitting pure machine assembly delivered a further 10x on top of that, roughly 100x over the original interpreter.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Two order-of-magnitude jumps in ~2 years means 'Wasm is too slow for the JVM' benchmarks older than a year are now worthless as decision inputs.
insights.quote: We improved performance 10x by using the compiler to Java bytecode. And I recently released a new compiler which instead produces a pure assembly that again increases 10x performance again on Prism
insights.locator: Real-World Use Cases: Doom and Prism

insights.claim: WebAssembly bytecode and Java bytecode are structurally similar enough that a direct near-one-pass translation works, the only real mismatch being Wasm's structured control flow versus the JVM's unstructured control flow — and that direction is easy because it moves from a more constrained to a less constrained environment.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: The low translation impedance explains why JVM Wasm runtimes caught up so fast, and why the same trick will not port cheaply to VMs with less permissive control flow.
insights.quote: WebAssembly has structured control flow, while it's unstructured on the JVM

insights.claim: Once WebAssembly functions are translated into generated Java functions they get picked up by the C1 and C2 just-in-time compilers and, after enough iterations, approach the performance of native compilers targeting machine assembly.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Decades of HotSpot JIT investment become a free performance dividend for Wasm-on-JVM — a moat non-JVM Wasm hosts do not get.
insights.quote: they will start to get optimized by the just-in-time compiler, C1 and C2. And they will eventually become very, very fast on the JVM after a number of iterations and almost match the performance of native compilers

insights.claim: For fixed WebAssembly payloads such as an embedded QuickJS engine, the preferred deployment pattern is to compile Wasm to Java bytecode once ahead of time and ship the frozen bytecode, avoiding the thin reflection layer that runtime linking requires in restricted environments.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Build-time compilation makes Wasm viable where reflection is banned (Native Image, hardened runtimes), widening the addressable deployment surface.
insights.quote: this compiler can run both at runtime by linking the new program using a very, very thin layer of reflection

insights.claim: Rather than build a multi-pass compiler in-house over several years, the Chicory team compiled Cranelift — the Rust assembly-generating compiler behind Wasmtime — to WebAssembly itself and runs it inside Java to pre-compile user programs to machine assembly.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Wasm is now used to bootstrap Wasm tooling — a self-hosting loop that lets small teams import rivals' compiler R&D instead of funding their own.
insights.quote: we just took Cranelift, compiled it to WebAssembly itself, because it's just pure Rust, so we can reuse it in pure Java again

insights.claim: The Cranelift-based tier gives a pure-Java WebAssembly runtime essentially the same performance as Wasmtime, the state-of-the-art native runtime, without shipping or linking any native library.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Removes the last technical objection to keeping Wasm workloads inside the JVM process rather than shelling out to a native sidecar.
insights.quote: we have performance which are basically the very same as running on the Wasmtime, which is the state-of-the-art runtime in WebAssembly land

insights.claim: Users benchmarked the JVM WebAssembly runtime against Wasmtime and V8 rather than against Java baselines, and that competitive pressure — not the maintainers' own roadmap — is what forced the move to an assembly-emitting compiler.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: The comparison set for embedded runtimes is native engines, so 'good enough for Java' is not a defensible product position.
insights.quote: Okay, this is not as fast as Wasmtime. This is not as fast as V8 or the browser

themes.theme: Spec Maturity: Wasm 0.3, WasmGC and the Component Model

insights.claim: The WebAssembly core specification is essentially complete: the proposals needed to host more languages, including WasmGC garbage collection and multi-memory, are integrated into the 0.3 release referred to as Wasm 3.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Spec completion removes the 'still a moving target' objection that has been deferring enterprise adoption decisions.
insights.quote: It's called the Wasm 3, the 0.3 release and is the core foundation that enables anything else on top of Wasm.
insights.locator: Current State of WebAssembly and WASI

insights.claim: WasmGC opens the WebAssembly engine to garbage-collected languages such as Scala (via Scala.js), Kotlin and Dart, meaning those languages can now be executed on a JVM through a Wasm runtime.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Each GC language that reaches Wasm multiplies the reusable library pool for every Wasm host — a compounding network effect to track.
insights.quote: we have enabled a new class of languages to be able to run on top of the WebAssembly engine
insights.locator: Current State of WebAssembly and WASI

insights.claim: WASI Preview 2 is close to final and WASI Preview 3 integrates the Component Model, in which a program's interfaces are declared in a WIT file and the rest is generated so applications can be composed from WebAssembly components authored in different language ecosystems.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: If the Component Model lands, cross-language composition — not sandboxing — becomes Wasm's main commercial pitch; toolchain readiness is the gating variable to watch.
insights.quote: you can write the interfaces of your program in a WIT file, an interface file, and generate all the rest to compose your application with any other WebAssembly components
insights.locator: Current State of WebAssembly and WASI

insights.claim: A server-side JVM WebAssembly runtime deliberately implements only the subset of the specification that makes sense off the browser, rather than chasing full spec parity, and has only an initial WasmGC implementation.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Server-side and browser Wasm are forking in practice; spec-conformance scores are a misleading proxy for server-side fitness.
insights.quote: In Chicory, we are compatible with all those specs, or most of them, whatever makes sense on the server side.
insights.locator: Current State of WebAssembly and WASI

themes.theme: Where Wasm Already Won: CDN Edge and Plugin Architectures

insights.claim: Cloudflare, Fastly and Akamai all run customer code on WebAssembly for their edge compute offerings — Cloudflare's Durable Objects and Fastly's and Akamai's compute-at-the-edge products — because no other technology delivers that density and provider-side security for untrusted workloads.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Edge multi-tenancy economics are already Wasm-dependent; any credible challenger to the CDN compute layer has to match the Wasm density curve.
insights.quote: there is no other technology that is able to run this kind of workload in such small armor and with such a high density and security for the provider

insights.claim: WebAssembly's adoption fight is over in the browser front end and at the CDN edge — those are settled wins — and the remaining contested ground is the server-side and JVM embedding market.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Frame Wasm bets by segment: edge is an installed base to monetize, server-side JVM is the growth option still up for grabs.
insights.quote: So, that's where WebAssembly already won.

insights.claim: Helm 4 integrates the Wazero WebAssembly runtime so users can customize Helm's behavior by injecting Wasm plug-ins, making Wasm the extension mechanism for core Kubernetes tooling.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Wasm is becoming the default plugin ABI for infrastructure tools; incumbents shipping bespoke plugin systems face rising switching pressure.
insights.quote: Wazero is integrated in Helm 4 so that you can customize the behavior of Helm by injecting WebAssembly plug-ins

insights.claim: Trino, the Java-based SQL query engine for large data volumes, has run CPython user-defined functions in production on the Chicory WebAssembly runtime since its 1.0 release roughly two years ago.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: A production-proven Python-UDF-in-Java-database pattern is a template every JVM data platform can now copy at low cost.
insights.quote: Chicory powers CPython UDF functions in Trinodp

insights.claim: WebAssembly's real adoption path is as invisible plumbing beneath libraries rather than as a headline technology — Microcks users were being taught JavaScript scripting in a workshop without realizing a Wasm engine was underneath.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Wasm penetration will be systematically undercounted by developer surveys; measure it through dependency graphs of runtimes, not self-reported usage.
insights.quote: It won't go for the hype, but it will power underlying libraries but would be otherwise impossible.

insights.claim: Red Hat's stated pattern of 'write Rust and deploy anywhere' is being applied to feature-flag systems such as OpenFeature and Spotify Confidence, where a shared subset of flag-evaluation rules is written in Rust and executed through a WebAssembly runtime inside Java, Go, Swift and native SDKs.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Any product that must keep identical business logic across many language SDKs is a natural Wasm conversion candidate — a repeatable adoption vector to screen for.
insights.quote: they will write Rust and deploy anywhere

insights.claim: Automerge, the local-first CRDT library, solves the many-SDK problem by writing the core in Rust and compiling it to WebAssembly, giving it bindings in essentially every language without per-language ports.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: The 'one Rust core, many language surfaces' pattern is now the default architecture for cross-platform libraries — a leading indicator of Rust plus Wasm toolchain demand.
insights.quote: We build Automerge in Rust, and you just compile it as WebAssembly, and then you have so many options in pretty much all the languages

insights.claim: Cloud isolation is splitting into two camps — microVMs such as Firecracker versus WebAssembly — and on the Wasm side SpinKube's pitch is packing Wasm jobs into the leftover memory and CPU slack of Kubernetes nodes.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: Wasm competes for the bin-packing remainder rather than replacing VMs outright — its cloud TAM is utilization recovery, which is a smaller but stickier wedge.
insights.quote: in the small cracks of the space that you still have in terms of memory and CPU, you can just run a couple of WebAssembly jobs

themes.theme: JavaScript and Ruby Beachheads on the JVM

insights.claim: There is no non-deprecated way to run JavaScript inside a Java application today — Rhino and Nashorn are both deprecated and GraalJS requires being on GraalVM — which leaves QuickJS compiled to WebAssembly as the only general-purpose option.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: A capability vacuum in the largest enterprise language runtime is exactly where a new runtime standard gets locked in; QuickJS-on-Wasm is the default winner by absence of alternatives.
insights.quote: there is basically no way to run JavaScript inside the Java application without using a non-deprecated library because Rhino and Nashorn, they are both deprecated, and the only alternative is GraalJS

insights.claim: Shopify's heavy investment in QuickJS and its Javy project — built so merchants can customize shops with WebAssembly functions — is what made embedding a JavaScript engine into other ecosystems, including Java, cheap for third parties.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: One commerce vendor's internal extensibility investment is now infrastructure for unrelated ecosystems — a reminder that Wasm tooling spillovers accrue outside the funder.
insights.quote: thanks to the Javy project by Shopify is extremely easy to get it to run on WebAssembly

insights.claim: Microcks, a CNCF API-mocking project built as a Spring Boot application, integrated user-pluggable JavaScript behavior very quickly by hooking up QuickJS running on WebAssembly instead of building or embedding a JS engine itself.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Time-to-integration measured in days, not quarters, is the adoption metric that will pull Wasm into mainstream Java frameworks.
insights.quote: They wanted to integrate with an external language to let the user plug in their behavior, and we hooked up very quickly QuickJS and provided the functionality.

insights.claim: The Rhino project, trying to keep pace with the latest ECMAScript specification which now includes WebAssembly, asked the Chicory team to become the WebAssembly engine behind Rhino.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Legacy JS engines outsourcing their Wasm layer signals that maintaining an independent Wasm implementation is no longer economic for smaller projects — consolidation onto a few engines.
insights.quote: they ask us to be the WebAssembly engine behind the Rhino

insights.claim: Prism, the C-language Ruby parser under the Ruby GitHub organization that powers JRuby, has been compiled to WebAssembly and executed from Java since day zero of the Chicory project, letting any JVM parse Ruby syntax without installing native libraries.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: The Ruby community consolidating on one official parser plus Wasm distribution is the template for how a language ecosystem exports its front end to other runtimes.
insights.quote: we have been compiling this Ruby parser to Wasm and executing it in Java since day zero
insights.locator: Real-World Use Cases: Doom and Prism

themes.theme: Hard Limits: No Concurrency, Translation Tax

insights.claim: WebAssembly has no notion of concurrency or parallelism today, so any workload whose performance depends on using multiple cores is a no-go on Wasm alone.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: This single gap caps Wasm's addressable server workloads to single-threaded or externally orchestrated tasks — the threads proposal is the unlock to watch.
insights.quote: it doesn't have any notion of concurrency or parallelism. This is a no-go as of today.

insights.claim: The absence of threading is being inverted into a feature: developers who need a hard guarantee that code runs on exactly one thread drop it into WebAssembly and get that guarantee plus sandbox safety for free, with orchestration handled in the host language.
insights.speaker: Olimpiu Pop
insights.so_what: A missing feature is being sold as a determinism guarantee — a pattern worth watching, since fixing threads could remove a use case as well as unlock one.
insights.quote: he wanted to have guaranteed that it's running only on one thread, he just dropped everything in WebAssembly

insights.claim: Compiling a Java application to WebAssembly with GraalVM's WebImage and then translating it back to Java bytecode to run on a JVM is technically possible today but is discouraged, because every translation step adds bindings and embeddings that make the program slower.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Each Wasm hop carries a compounding performance tax, so architectures that chain multiple Wasm translations will underperform their benchmarks.
insights.quote: each and every translation increases a little bit of the number of bindings and the number of embeddings that you need to run the regional program, making it slower

insights.claim: WebAssembly's opinionated memory model, which isolates the guest's memory from the host, makes it the right fit specifically for running software you do not trust or cannot afford to have crash the machine.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Scope Wasm's value to the untrusted-code problem; pitching it as a general performance runtime invites the concurrency objection that kills deals.
insights.quote: in any application where you want to run a piece of software which you are not confident about, or you really don't want to crash your machine around that piece of code, WebAssembly is a perfect fit

themes.theme: Governance: Chicory Forks to Endive Under Bytecode Alliance

insights.claim: The Chicory WebAssembly runtime is being forked under the Bytecode Alliance organization as a new project named Endive, with the same maintainers carrying over and a first release expected very soon.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Anyone with a Chicory dependency should plan a rename migration and track which artifact the maintainers actually ship against.
insights.quote: we are going to fork Chicory under the Bytecode Alliance organization, and the new name is going to be Endive

insights.claim: The fork happened because negotiations with Dylibso failed to produce a clean transfer of the project while keeping the Chicory name, forcing a rename rather than a handover.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: A vendor losing its flagship runtime's maintainer base to a foundation fork is a real commercial event for that vendor — watch which name the ecosystem's downstream projects follow.
insights.quote: We have tried to talk with Dylibso. Unfortunately, we couldn't make a deal for clean transfer of the project keeping the name

insights.claim: The stated rationale for moving to foundation governance is that contributors are unwilling to contribute to a single company's project, so neutrality under a foundation is expected to increase individual participation.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Corporate-owned open source runtimes carry a structural contributor discount; foundation moves are a leading indicator of a project trying to escape it.
insights.quote: we go under a foundation so that everyone would be free to contribute instead of contributing to a single company

insights.claim: Moving under the Bytecode Alliance also imposes that foundation's more restrictive rules, which the maintainers frame as making the JVM WebAssembly runtime more secure and more available rather than as overhead.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Foundation compliance regimes are becoming a security-assurance signal buyers can price, not just governance paperwork.
insights.quote: we are going to comply with all the more restrictive rules of Bytecode Alliance that is helping us making the runtime as secure and available as possible

insights.claim: The runtime was built safety-first and performance-second, and everything running on top of it depends on a very limited number of external libraries that are themselves built on the Java standard library — with the generated code usually smaller than the original Wasm module.
insights.speaker: Andrea Peruffo
insights.so_what: Near-zero dependency counts are becoming a purchasing criterion as supply-chain attacks rise; libraries like Gunnar Morling's Hardwood are marketed on the same axis.
insights.quote: even the code that gets generated is usually much smaller than the original Wasm
